The donation went to the Too Extreme for Idaho Political Action Committ
items.body: The Boise Temple of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints as seen on Feb. 5, 2025. (Photo by Otto Kitsinger for Idaho Capital Sun) The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints has donated $1 million to an Idaho political action committee, or PAC, opposing the abortion rights initiative on the ballot this November. The donation went to the Too Extreme for Idaho Political Action Committee, which opposes the initiative. “While The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints remains neutral toward political candidates, it actively addresses ballot initiatives it believes carry significant moral consequences,” the church said in a statement. “Accordingly, the Church has joined a coalition of like-minded organizations and individuals in Idaho to dedicate resources toward defeating Proposition 1.” Supporters and opponents of Idaho’s abortion rights initiative, Prop 1, have raised millions If passed, the voter initiative would repeal Idaho’s abortion laws, enumerate rights related to reproductive health, and create liability protections for healthcare providers who provide abortion and other reproductive healthcare. The Idaho Falls radio station NewsTalk 107.9 first reported the donation on Thursday. The Idaho Capital Sun confirmed the donation with a spokesperson for the church on Friday. The large donation comes after Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador published an opinion in August that says churches are allowed to donate money to political campaigns — including for and against Proposition 1 — without disclosing their donors, as long as they don’t ask members to donate specifically for the campaign, Boise State Public Radio reported. Leaders from the church, widely known as the Mormon church, issued a letter against Prop 1 in September, the Salt Lake Tribune reported. The letter was read to congregations last month, the church’s assistant communications director Brian Whitlock said in an email. “Our long-held stance on abortion remains clear and unchanged,” the four-member U.S. Central Area Presidency of the LDS Church wrote in the letter. The church, which opposes elective abortions, posted its stance on abortion online . It allows for possible exemptions in cases of rape and incest, if a “competent physician determines that the life or health of the mother is in serious jeopardy,” or a “competent physician determines that the fetus has severe defects that will not allow the baby to survive beyond birth.” “Even these exceptions do not automatically justify abortion,” the statement said. “Abortion is a most serious matter. It should be considered only after the persons responsible have received confirmation through prayer.” Idaho’s abortion ban allows the procedure to prevent the death of the mother and in cases of rape and incest in the first trimester with a police report. Doctors who provide abortions outside of those exemptions face felony penalties, including minimum prison time, and potential civil lawsuits brought by family members of the aborted fetus. Groups attached to Catholic organizations have contributed $7,161 to the Too Extreme for Idaho PAC, campaign finance reporting shows. The Roman Catholic Diocese of Boise contributed $2,000, and Catholic fraternal groups, called Knights of Columbus Councils, contributed the rest, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. items.body: President Donald Trump signed an executive order to allow dyed diesel on highways and prohibit the Internal Revenue Service from imposing the typical penalties for doing so. Some state restrictions remain on the fuel, but on Friday, Idaho Gov. Brad Little relaxed the Gem State's inspections of the fuel during harvest. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor) Idaho Gov. Brad Little signed an executive order Friday to suspend for 30 days state inspections of dyed diesel fuel in an attempt to lower costs for farmers and ranchers, according to the governor’s office. With election pressure mounting, states move to suspend fuel taxes Dyed diesel is diesel fuel with red dye in it and is exempt from federal and state motor fuel taxes. The tax-exempt fuel is only meant for certain approved off-road uses, such as for farming equipment, construction equipment and home heating. The dye helps regulators enforce this requirement. Idaho’s average diesel price was around $6.41 per gallon as of Friday, according to AAA fuel prices. Prices for oil products have risen this year largely because of restrictions on ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz amid the U.S. and Israel’s war with Iran, which have disrupted global supply chains. Diesel supplies have been in particularly short supply, NPR reported, and Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries have also affected global supplies. On Monday, President Donald Trump signed an executive order to allow dyed diesel on highways and prohibit the Internal Revenue Service from imposing the typical penalties for doing so. Some state restrictions remain on the fuel. President Donald Trump hands off a newly signed executive order waiving federal taxes on red-dyed diesel to aide Natalie Harp during a 2026 midterms rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, on Oct. 5, 2026, at the Nebraska State Fairgrounds with thousands in attendance. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner) Little’s order signed Friday directs Idaho State Police and the Idaho Transportation Department to suspend inspection for dyed diesel while the agencies review Idaho’s policies and procedures, his office announced in a press release. The review will consider other state’s approach to dyed diesel enforcement and the agencies will make recommendations to Little for “efficient, effective, and practical inspection,” the release said. Little said in the press release that the timing of the order is meant to ease costs during harvest season. “Idaho farmers and ranchers work hard to feed our families, our country, and the world,” Little said in the release. “President Trump has made cutting red tape a priority, and Idaho is doing the same. We will continue looking for ways to give our farmers, ranchers, and working men and women on the road more freedom to do what they do best.” Legislative leaders in written statements said they supported the governor’s decision. “Idaho farmers and ranchers are facing high costs across the board, and expensive diesel is adding to the pressure during harvest,” Senate President Pro Tempore Kelly Anthon, R-Declo, said in the release. “This order provides some immediate relief while giving the state time to review these requirements and find a practical approach that supports our producers without adding unnecessary costs or red tape.” House Speaker Mike Moyle , R-Star, said suspending the inspections while the state reviews its policies “is a practical approach that puts common sense first and gives Idaho producers one less thing to worry about during harvest.” YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE. items.body: Collecting payments and convincing school districts to sign binding agreements to cover the Idaho School Benefit Trust’s $13 million shortfall has been a little bit more challenging than anticipated, Idaho Department of Insurance Director Dean Cameron told EdNews on Friday. It’s been two weeks since the Fourth District Court named Cameron the rehabilitator of the trust , vesting in him full control of the trust and its assets, including the authority to liquidate assets to pay claims and liabilities. “Our focus is singular in attempting to make sure that all the claims that school district employees incurred are appropriately processed and paid for,” Cameron said. The trust, which more than 100 school districts and charter schools participated in during the 2025-26 benefit year, ran out of money this year and recorded a deficit of $10.5 million at the end of May. Blue Cross of Idaho, the trust third-party administrator for that benefit year, agreed to make an $11.9 million loan with 6% interest to pay off claims through Aug. 31. As rehabilitator of the trust, Cameron and the department have been tasked with collecting contributions from the member employers to pay off the loan, called a surplus note, to Blue Cross. Cameron was unable to share many details about what the department has learned since gaining access to the trust’s books and records on Sept. 24, but described some of the complications with corralling the more than 100 members into agreeing to either pay a lump sum or sign a 12-month binding contract agreeing to make monthly payments to cover their share of the shortfall. “Frankly, it’d have been easier for everybody if everybody paid a lump sum,” Cameron said. “But we acknowledge that for some districts that was not going to be possible, and so Blue Cross offered the monthly option in that case.” He said there have been some miscommunications and some rumors. “I think in part because maybe school districts were somewhat surprised,” Cameron said. “They shouldn’t have been, but they were.” Dean Cameron, director of the Idaho Department of Insurance, speaks to a lawmaker after an Idaho Health Insurers Working Group meeting on Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026, in Boise. items.body: The exterior of the Idaho Statehouse as seen on Jan. 14, 2026, in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho state revenues beat their forecast for the third straight month and are now more than $90 million ahead of projections to begin Fiscal Year 2027, Gov. Brad Little announced Friday. For September, general fund revenues exceeded their forecast by $39 million, or 7%, according to the September General Fund Revenue Report issued by the Idaho Division of Financial Management. Idaho Republican Gov. Brad Little gives his State of the State Address from the House chambers on Jan. 12, 2026, at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho’s state government runs on a fiscal year calendar that begins July 1 each year. Through the first three months of Fiscal Year 2027, state revenues are now up by $90.3 million, or 6.8%. The surging revenues in this year’s state budget are a stark contrast to last year, when Little and Idaho state legislators approved near across-the-board budget cuts for almost all state agencies, programs and departments to pay for federal tax cuts President Donald Trump signed into law through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and to ensure the state passed a balanced budget, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. State revenues were also up in July and August. “Idaho’s strong revenue growth is encouraging and reflects the strength of our economy, but we must remain disciplined and make spending decisions based on what we can responsibly sustain,” Little said in a written statement Friday afternoon. “The difficult decisions we made last year put us in a stronger fiscal position, and we need to continue prioritizing the investments that matter most to Idahoans while protecting our long-term financial stability.” Income tax withholdings are driver of state revenue increase Individual income tax withholdings are a big part of the revenue increase. The September General Fund Revenue Report said individual income tax collections are up 18.3% fiscal year to date. “It appears that employees are getting lots of hours of work and that there may be some bonus activity being paid by employers,” Idaho Division of Financial Management officials wrote in the September revenue report. items.body: The mental health of our children is on everyone’s mind, including school leaders. That’s why 10 rural districts and charter schools jumped at the chance to apply for mental health support through Idaho’s Rural Health Transformation Program. The plans included counseling, telehealth, and behavioral health coordinators to help students and families connect with care. Their work was wasted when a Republican-only interim committee voted to shut down the opportunity and redirect $1.2 million. The documented need was high. In Notus, 46% of surveyed junior high and high school students identified mental health as a concern, and the district sought $60,000 for a coordinator serving students from preschool through 12th grade. Aberdeen wanted to expand counseling and wellness services in a community where some care is 20 to 50 minutes away. The decision is hard to understand, but it fits a pattern from the Republican supermajority: cutting investments in mental health. Last year, Idaho eliminated Assertive Community Treatment, or ACT, along with peer support services, as years of tax cuts for the wealthy left less money for essential services. ACT provided intensive, mobile care for people with severe mental illness. Providers and law enforcement warned that people would end up in crisis without those supports. Soon, visits to eastern Idaho crisis centers had increased by 34% in December and 43% in January compared with the year before. Providers reported rising hospitalizations and more pressure on jails. Four former ACT patients died after the program was cut, compared with one reported death during the previous 18 months. After months of warnings and advocacy from mental health practitioners, lawmakers pieced together one-time funding to bring ACT and peer support back. That meant providers had to fight to restore services instead of focusing on patients in their communities. But the future of those services remains uncertain. These cuts were not just cruel. They were shortsighted from a budget perspective, too. Providers estimated ACT cost less than $100 per patient per day, while untreated illness can lead to repeated hospitalizations, court hearings, and jail stays that cost taxpayers far more. When elected officials disregard the health and safety of our communities, there should be accountability. The Rural Health Transformation Committee is made up of eight Republican lawmakers, including Reps. Dori Healey and Dustin Manwaring. Both are now up for reelection in two of the most competitive legislative districts in Idaho. Voters in those districts should take a hard look at this record. Blocking mental health resources for rural families after Idaho has already seen the consequences of cutting care is the kind of decision that should carry real political consequences. The Republicans who made this decision had the chance to learn from what happened. Now voters do too.

(Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun) In 2007, Idaho lawmakers passed a law to make English the state’s official language. That law, which is still on the books , requires English to be used as “the sole language of government.” But it lists many exceptions to its requirement that government documents be in English, such as for law enforcement or for “public health and safety needs,” to ensure public schools can teach students who are learning English and to ensure colleges and so universities can “pursue educational purposes.” 2026 Voter Guide Dates to know, how-to instructions and candidate surveys for Idaho’s top contested races. Read More In this year’s general election on Nov. 3, Idaho voters will decide on whether to amend the state’s constitution to declare English as the state’s official language. But what isn’t immediately clear, some say, is whether the amendment will end existing exemptions in state law that allow languages other than English to be used by government agencies. The proposed constitutional amendment’s only exception allows the government to use other languages when required by federal law, such as in schools and, in some cases, election administration. “It’s not entirely clear, honestly, how much it would change things,” said University of Idaho law professor Richard Seamon, who has taught at the school for 30 years. The proposed amendment, passed by the Idaho Legislature to be placed on the ballot through House Joint Resolution 6 in 2025 , calls for English to be used in “all public proceedings, public documents, public instruction, and any other public acts of any public institution of the state of Idaho.” Here’s what the amendment will look like on your ballot: .indent2Container { margin-left: 1em; border-left: solid 1px var(--brand_one); padding-left: 2em; } “Shall Article X of the Constitution of the State of Idaho be amended by the addition of a new Section 8, to provide that the English language shall be the official language for the state of Idaho, and to further provide that, except as required by federal law, English shall be used in all public proceedings, public documents, public instruction, and any other public acts of any public institution in the state of Idaho?” To pass, the amendment needs support from at least 50% of voters. items.body: The Idaho Public Charter School Commission approved applications for two new schools Thursday — with some conditions. Doral Academy of Idaho, a K-8 charter school in Meridian, plans to add grades 9-12 at a second campus. Elevate Academy, a network of career-technical charters, is also preparing a new CTE-focused school serving grades 6-12 in Pocatello. Before they open, however, school leaders must prove to the charter commission that they have balanced operating budgets along with lease or purchase agreements for their buildings. They must also hand over copies of all grants, loans and contracts they’ve secured to fund and operate the schools. The charter commission unanimously voted to approve the schools with conditions. If the conditions aren’t satisfied, school openings could be delayed or the commission’s approval of their applications could be revoked. Doral Academy Preparatory Doral Academy will add a second campus, also in Meridian, that serves middle and high schoolers. The new school, Doral Academy Preparatory, will be 6-12 while the current school moves to K-5. Doral Academy is an “arts-integration” school, which means it uses arts as a method of instruction in all subjects, said Sara Frost, chairwoman of the charter’s board of directors. “We want to continue growing that into a high school experience that will continue to be a very vibrant and enriching education for our students.” Doral Academy leaders plan to launch the preparatory school next year, welcoming ninth-graders in the fall. Additional grades will be added in subsequent years after the new building in south Meridian is ready. The new school will have sports and house 840 students at full capacity, Frost told the commission. School leaders are banking on Meridian’s continued growth to fill the halls. Their presentation pointed to thousands of new residential units coming to south Meridian. items.body: Boise State University’s 10-year campus master plan has buy-in at City Hall. The Boise City Council signed off Tuesday on the university’s land use plan, the Idaho Statesman reported . This vote links the university’s plan and the city’s comprehensive land use plan. The 10-year university plan is designed to accommodate projected growth at Idaho’s largest four-year university — by adding 750 dormitory beds, 370 parking spaces and 270 staff members. The top priority is a $140 million science research building, a 90,000- to 110,000-square-foot project that would go up on the southern fringe of campus. Designed to address the university’s shortage of research space, the new building is scheduled to come online in 2029. The dorm space will focus on two areas of need: housing for first-year students and graduate student housing. City Hall will still get a say on specific projects. “While we’re approving a master plan, we’re not approving any specific plans,” said council member Jimmy Hallyburton, according to a Statesman report on the Tuesday meeting. “Those things would have to come back before council.” More reading: Click here for an in-depth April article on Boise State’s 10-year plan.

items.body: A federal school choice super PAC announced Thursday that it has endorsed Gov. Brad Little for reelection. The AFC Victory Fund, a political action committee affiliated with the American Federation for Children, stated in a press release that Little has supported “significant school choice expansion,” citing the $50 million Parental Choice Tax Credit, the Idaho Launch grant program and opting in to the federal Education Freedom Tax Credit. Tommy Schultz, CEO of the AFC Victory Fund, said Little has empowered families to “choose the education that best fits their child’s needs, abilities and aspirations.” “Idahoans are demanding school choice, and elected leaders are responding,” Schultz said in the press release. “We are proud to endorse Governor Brad Little for reelection and look forward to working alongside him and other Idaho leaders committed to delivering school choice for every family.” Gov. In 2023, Little signed House Bill 24 , creating the Idaho Launch grant program for graduating high school seniors. Students can apply for up to $8,000 in tuition support for in-demand career programs. “Together, LAUNCH and the PCTC made Idaho the first state to offer education freedom from kindergarten through career,” the press release stated. This year, Little signed an executive order opting Idaho into a federal school choice tax credit under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The AFC Victory Fund’s press release this week used similar language in Little’s February statement. “Idaho is proud to be the only state offering education freedom from kindergarten through career,” Little said in a February press release. “My executive order strengthens our commitment to ensuring every parent has the opportunity to choose the education environment that best fits their child.” The American Federation for Children in April terminated the Idaho Federation for Children PAC, which spent $432,923 in 2024 to elect school choice candidates, and is now using the federal super PAC AFC Victory Fund to make independent expenditures in Idaho’s elections. The super PAC spent $105,517 on the May primaries. While the school choice group is supporting Little, the statewide Idaho Education Association teachers’ union in April issued a vote of no-confidence in the governor.

items.body: For 80 minutes Tuesday night, Terri Pickens and John Stegner agreed about almost everything. Especially Brad Little. Sharing a stage at a Boise junior high school auditorium, Pickens and Stegner took turns laying out a litany of criticisms. Little is too deferential to President Donald Trump. Little compromises too much with House Speaker Mike Moyle and other conservative lawmakers. Little is wrong on private school choice. Wrong about opening Idaho to, potentially, thousands of tons of nuclear waste shipments . Weak on public lands. Too often silent. Pickens, an attorney, and Stegner, a retired judge, presented a case for the prosecution. An audience of about 150 people murmured their approval, applauded on occasion, and snickered at the zingers. Little provided no defense. The two-term governor was a no-show for the League of Women Voters forum . A folding chair, reserved for Little, sat vacant. A bottle of water remained unopened. Pickens, a Democrat, and Stegner, an independent, are crisscrossing the state. In stump speeches and joint appearances, they are desperately trying to take the fight to the incumbent. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) This year, Idaho voters have a lot to decide on: Who will be the state’s next governor or U.S. senator? Should two constitutional amendments pass? Should voters pass their own law to repeal the state’s abortion ban? 2026 Voter Guide Dates to know, how-to instructions and candidate surveys for Idaho’s top contested races. Read More But in the mix is a poll that the Idaho Legislature called for: What should be the state’s official gun? Idaho, a Republican supermajority-controlled state, has strong protections for gun ownership — such as not requiring permits for concealed carry in city limits. The state Legislature considered a bill this year to allow members of the public to carry concealed guns inside parts of courthouses that aren’t meant for court, like offices for county commissioners and clerks. The advisory question on the ballot this year asks voters to weigh in on the Legislature’s possible decision to declare a firearm — out of a mix of well-known Western and American guns — as Idaho’s official state gun. If Idaho declared a state gun, the recognition would grow the list of officially declared state symbols , like the state flower, the syringa; the state gem, the star garnet; or the state amphibian, the Idaho giant salamander. Ten other states have declared state guns , according to the National Rifle Association, a prominent gun lobbying group. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Idaho lawmaker hopes the advisory question will boost voter turnout One of the lawmakers behind the push for the ballot question, Rep. Jason Monks, R-Meridian, said he thought it might drum up voter turnout during a year when many consequential issues are on the ballot. In election years when the president isn’t on the ballot, like this year, fewer voters tend to participate. “Voter turnout is always important,” he said in an interview. “… When you have a lot of voter apathy, I think we don’t get as good of results as we could if we had an informed electorate that was actually out and voting.” The votes won’t be the final say. “The results,” the bill says, “will guide the Legislature as to which gun shall be designated the state gun of Idaho.” Idaho Senate Majority Leader Lori Den Hartog, R-Meridian, and Idaho House Majority Leader Jason Monks, R-Meridian, walk Gov. Brad Little out of the House chambers after the governor delivered his State of the State Address on Jan. 12, 2026, at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) But Monks said this is the only time he knows of when the state sought public input before designating a state item. Monks acknowledges that not everyone loves the idea of declaring a state gun. “I don’t think you can make everybody always happy. The majority of people in Idaho do have guns,” he said. “We have a pretty high percentage of gun ownership in our state. And so I think it reflects the fact that Idaho is a very gun-friendly state, and that it is an important part of our culture in many aspects.” He stressed that the push for the ballot question didn’t take much time. “I had some people ask me, ‘How come this is your priority?’ I’m like, ‘Well, this isn’t my priority. (Photo by Laura Guido/Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho’s top-ranking federal law enforcement official, U.S. Attorney Bart Davis, announced his retirement Wednesday following a long, influential legal and political career in Idaho . ‘The best job I ever had’: Bart Davis returns as Idaho’s chief federal litigator Davis, who is 71 and in
items.body: U.S. Attorney for the District of Idaho Bart Davis in his Boise office. (Photo by Laura Guido/Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho’s top-ranking federal law enforcement official, U.S. Attorney Bart Davis, announced his retirement Wednesday following a long, influential legal and political career in Idaho . ‘The best job I ever had’: Bart Davis returns as Idaho’s chief federal litigator Davis, who is 71 and in his second term as U.S. attorney for the District of Idaho, will retire Oct. 17, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Idaho said. “I am unable to overstate the privilege it has been to work with the dedicated and remarkable women and men of the U.S. Attorney’s Office,” Davis said in a written statement. “These great lawyers and support staff faithfully enforce the law, work to keep Idaho and our country safe, support our law enforcement partners and protect the civil rights of others. I am proud of the work they do every day.” President Donald Trump nominated Davis for U.S. attorney for the District of Idaho last year, and the U.S. Senate confirmed Davis on Oct. 7, 2025 – exactly one year before Davis announced his retirement. Davis previously served as U.S. attorney for the District of Idaho from 2017 to 2021 during Trump’s first term. Prior to serving as U.S. attorney, Davis practiced law in Idaho Falls and served in the Idaho Senate for 19 years. Davis, a Republican, served as Senate majority leader for 15 years, where he was regarded as a powerful and intelligent legislative leader. “Bart Davis has served the State of Idaho and our country with distinction throughout a remarkable career,” Idaho Gov. Brad Little said in a written statement. “His sound legal judgment, deep knowledge of Idaho and unwavering commitment to doing what is right have been invaluable to our state.” Davis also served as co-chairman of the 2021 Idaho Commission for Reapportionment , which was charged with redrawing Idaho’s congressional and legislative boundaries following the 2020 census to ensure political representation is proportional. During a 2025 interview with the Idaho Capital Sun, Davis called serving as U.S. attorney, “the best job I ever had.” “… to work with these people who are genuinely trying to even-handedly apply the laws of the United States of America,” Davis said. “It impressed me then, and it impresses me now.” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Governor says Davis strengthened relationship between Justice Department and Idaho Idaho Gov. Brad Little gives a press conference after delivering his annual State of the State address on Jan. 6, 2025, in the Lincoln Auditorium in the Idaho Capitol. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Idaho is responsible for prosecuting federal crimes in Idaho, defends the United States in civil cases and collects debts owed to the United States, the office said. In the past year under Davis’ leadership, the office said it has filed 298 criminal charges, including 103 drug trafficking cases, 89 violent crimes cases, 69 immigration cases and 22 fraud cases. “During his time as U.S. Attorney for Idaho, Bart strengthened the relationship between Idaho and the U.S. Department of Justice and represented our state with integrity and professionalism,” Little said. “ We will miss his counsel, his wisdom and his steady leadership. I am grateful for Bart’s many years of service and friendship, and I wish him all the best as he enters retirement and has more time to enjoy with his wife, children and grandchildren.” Davis and his wife, Marion, have six children and 14 grandchildren. Davis and Marion recently celebrated their 50th wedding anniversary. YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE. SUPPORT

items.body: Independent U.S. Senate candidate Todd Achilles, left, and Independent Leadership Council co-founder Adam Brandon speak about Achilles' commitment to not caucus with either major party, to only serve two terms, hold public town halls and participate in debates if elected. Achilles held the press conference on Oct. 7, 2026, at the Idaho Statehouse in Boise. (Photo by Laura Guido/Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho independent U.S. Senate candidate Todd Achilles on Wednesday pledged to not caucus with either party if he’s elected. 2026 Voter Guide The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote. Read More Achilles, who served in the Idaho Legislature as a Democrat before announcing his independent run for U.S. Senate, is running against incumbent Republican Sen. Jim Risch , who’s in his 18th year as a senator. Achilles was joined at the Idaho state Capitol in Boise by Adam Brandon, the co-founder of a national advocacy organization promoting independent candidates called the Independent Leadership Council . Achilles also committed to serve a maximum of two terms, hold town halls in each of Idaho’s 44 counties every two years, and to engage in public debates. Brandon previously was president of FreedomWorks, which helped tea party candidates get elected to office. That organization dissolved in 2024 , Politico reported. “Every vote that he casts, both parties are going to have to come to him for his vote to represent the state of Idaho, and I think that is incredibly, incredibly powerful,” Brandon said. Idaho US Senate candidates weigh in on tariffs, Iran War, federal spending and more In the letter Achilles signed to make these commitments, he said the U.S. Senate rules would still guarantee him a committee seat despite not caucusing with the major parties. The two independent U.S. senators — Angus King of Maine and Bernie Sanders of Vermont — both caucus with Senate Democrats. When King won his election in 2012, he announced he would caucus with the Democrats because it would allow him to participate more in the committee process, PBS News reported at the time. Committee assignments are largely decided by party leaders and then formally voted on by the entire Senate. During the event, Achilles also signed a sworn, notarized statement that would resign him from office in 2039 — meaning if elected, he would only be able to serve two, six-year terms. A spokesman for the Achilles campaign said the letter will be sent to either the governor’s office or secretary of state to keep. “We’re serious about this,” Achilles said Wednesday. “That’s it. I don’t want to spend more than 12 years in D.C. I love Idaho’s mountains. I want to get back here and get my skis on and do what I love doing. So two terms. That’s it.” YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE. According to an online petition , members of Timberline’s football team used Snapchat to “call for a female student to be raped and killed.” Police began investigating the reported threats last week after Timberline officials contacted Boise police. items.body: Hundreds of Idahoans gathered in the rotunda of the Idaho Capitol on Jan. 12, 2026, to protest proposed cuts to the state's Medicaid program. The protest, organized by Idaho Voices for Children, took place before the governor's State of the State Address. (Photo by Christina Lords/Idaho Capital Sun) One thing we know for absolute certain in Idaho: Our people understand the value of Medicaid expansion. We voted to adopt Medicaid expansion in 2018 through ballot initiative started after years of inaction by the state Legislature, with more than 60 percent of Idaho voters supporting expanded healthcare access. When the state Legislature became very active in attempts to weaken and repeal that voter-approved expansion seemingly as soon as they could, Idahoans showed up. They traveled to Boise to let lawmakers know that the program was not a suggestion, but a mandate and more than 80,000 of our friends, family and neighbors relied on it. Idaho’s Medicaid work requirements start in January. Here’s how they will work. Some of the busiest days at the Capitol are when everyday Idahoans show up to have their voices heard on a healthcare bill when lawmakers have tried to repeal the program or institute confusing bureaucracy via work requirements. The halls are packed and hearing rooms overflow with Medicaid supporters who vastly outnumber those who advocate cuts at around 100-1 … and the one is very often not somebody from Idaho. Most Idahoans, myself included, don’t think much about the details of our health insurance until we need it. For someone with cancer, that could mean discovering at a doctor’s appointment, while scheduling a scan, or even in the middle of treatment or recovery that they no longer have Medicaid coverage due to the work requirements that will add red tape to the program starting in January. Then what? Do they delay treatment while trying to navigate the paperwork? Do they skip a follow-up appointment or prescription they can no longer afford? For most, there isn’t another insurance option waiting in the wings. These are Idahoans who already qualified for Medicaid, including people whose serious medical conditions should qualify them for a medical frailty exemption. Administrative red tape should not become another obstacle between a cancer patient and the care they need. When that happens, the consequences aren’t limited to the patient. Their families suffer too and local care providers must then care for somebody with no ability to pay the bill. It’s a terrible scenario and one Medicaid expansion has prevented from being widescale. This past session, House Bill 913 established the Jan. 1 start date for federally mandated work requirements. Medicaid proponents had requested a one-year extension to give the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare and our residents more time to learn about the changes and implementation. That did not happen, so we hope Idaho lawmakers grasp fully their responsibility to hold true to the promises they made clearly and often during all those Boise debates over work requirements. Then, they were firm in their convictions that no eligible person would ever be stripped of healthcare. Policymakers should be just as committed now to making work requirement exemptions clear and accessible as they were about putting them into law. Coverage losses from work requirements usually aren’t because someone suddenly became ineligible, but because eligible people get caught in paperwork, reporting requirements, missed notices or other government bureaucracy. items.body: Last summer, Mackay High history teacher Jess Johnson listened to an audiobook about the USS Indianapolis on a trip home from Mount Rushmore. The story sparked Johnson’s interest in Lt. Cmdr. Earl Henry Sr., the ship’s dentist and an avid bird painter and taxidermist. Henry died after a Japanese submarine torpedoed the ship in July 1945. The ship sank in about 12 minutes, killing hundreds of crewmen. Johnson learned that Henry’s son, Earl Henry Jr., sold prints of his father’s work. One painting, “American Eagle in the Pacific,” was completed on the ship before it sank. It depicts an eagle holding a tattered Japanese flag. Johnson ordered a copy. “A nd maybe 20 minutes after I purchased it, he calls me,” Johnson said. The phone call kicked off a lifelong friendship between Johnson and Henry Jr. — and became the foundation for a unit in Johnson’s military history class at Mackay High. It’s just one of dozens of out-of-the-box approaches Johnson uses to bring history to life for his students. “It’s our lives — it’s what happens,” he said. “I try to make the connection between the old and the new.” Click to view slideshow. A teacher in the making Johnson grew up on a farm outside of Preston. He wasn’t “that good of a student” but sports had an impact. By eighth grade, his coaches influenced him to become a teacher. After high school, he started a family and worked nights as a cheesemaker. He fit classes into a busy schedule. With six kids, it took Johnson seven years to finish his teaching degree. He graduated from Utah State University in 1990 and took his first teaching job in Yuma, Arizona, the next fall. He taught middle school classes and coached at the high school. Coaching came easy — teaching did not. “I was drowning, and my principal said, ‘You’re not a very good teacher and you’re not going to make it,'” Johnson recalls. He eventually partnered with a veteran teacher, who encouraged him to be himself, stay calm, and push through ups and downs. That changed everything, Johnson said. He soon fell in love with the job — and with history. ‘I said heck yeah’ Johnson eventually made his way back to Idaho. After nearly two decades teaching at American Falls High, he and some other coaches earned their master’s degrees. He took a job as principal of Mackay High Jr./Sr. School, where his children graduated. Johnson moved around after becoming an empty nester. Three years ago, his sons moved back to Mackay and asked him to move closer. “I said heck yeah,” Johnson said. He returned to Mackay to teach history, government, and coach junior high school football — and continue his emphasis on projects. ‘I don’t go into the book’ “My style is probably different than a traditional history teacher,” Johnson said. “I don’t go into the book. I teach the standards and whatever, but my whole career has been hands-on projects.” Johnson has come up with dozens of projects over the years that tie into his history lessons. Students dress up as Roman soldiers with homemade armor, make hardtack, make their own gas masks to test with a fog machine, dress up as 1920s flappers and set up a faux speakeasy. At 65, the projects keep Johnson excited about teaching. “It really makes it meaningful,” he said. For him, history is key to helping students understand the world around them. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Idahoans voting in November’s general election will decide whether to give the Idaho Legislature the sole power to regulate marijuana and other drugs — and eliminate their right to bring a citizen-led ballot initiative to do so. 2026 Voter Guide Dates to know, how-to instructions and candidate surveys for Idaho’s top contested races. Read More Currently, there are two ways in Idaho that marijuana, medical cannabis or other drugs can be legalized and regulated. First, the Idaho Legislature could pass a law to legalize it. Second, Idaho voters could legalize it by passing a ballot initiative. Who gets to decide is a big part of the debate over House Joint Resolution 4, or HJR 4 for short. House Joint Resolution 4 is a proposed amendment to the Idaho Constitution that would give the Idaho Legislature the sole authority and power to legalize marijuana (including medical marijuana), narcotics and other psychoactive substances. If a simple majority of voters vote “yes” for House Joint Resolution 4, Idahoans would not be allowed to bring a ballot initiative forward to legalize marijuana, medical cannabis, narcotics or other psychoactive substances. If voters vote “no” and don’t approve HJR 4, there would be no changes to the Idaho Constitution. That means Idahoans would still be able to use the ballot initiative process to legalize marijuana, narcotics or other psychoactive substances. Voters in several of Idaho’s neighboring states, including Washington, Oregon, Montana and Nevada, used ballot initiatives to legalize marijuana in those states. People have tried to do the same in Idaho. But so far, each effort has failed to meet the signature-gathering requirements to qualify for an election, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. David Adler is president of the nonprofit Alturas Institute in Idaho Falls. (Photo courtesy of David Adler) Adler has taught courses on government and the Constitution at all three of Idaho’s public universities and has spoken about HJR 4 this fall. “The more I speak on it, the more I realize people generally are of the belief that this is about regulating marijuana and they don’t understand that it has a far broader impact on their ability to resort to the initiative to exercise their rights,” Adler said. “Really, HJR 4 asks Idahoans to surrender both their rights and their powers to shape their future,” Adler said. He said a ballot initiative is a tool of democracy that the public has used to improve the state since the 1930s. Different ballot initiatives in Idaho have created the nonpartisan Idaho Fish and Game Commission, regulated dredge mining to protect clean water and created sunshine and transparency laws that provide for the disclosure of campaign finance reports and lobbying activity, Adler said Idaho voters should not give that power up permanently when nobody knows what future medical discoveries could come from drugs or psychoactive substances, Adler said, adding that coffee and tea are considered psychoactive substances. items.body: Joleen Noble, executive director of the Idaho Diaper Bank, says the nonprofit organization typically provides more than 75,000 diapers to children in need per month. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Diaper Bank) As a mother of two small children (ages 2 and 5), there’s no need to lecture Jolleen Noble of Meridian about the cost of diapers – which could run close to $200 a month per child. And there’s no need to talk to her about other paycheck-eating costs such as daycare, medical emergencies and clothing. She knows all about the challenges of making ends meet. Noble, of course, can’t solve all of the financial problems. But as the executive director of the Idaho Diaper Bank , she’s providing some welcome relief in at least one area. And there are no forms to fill out, or financial statements to submit. “People who need diapers need our help,” she said. There are limits. Noble’s nonprofit organization will provide up to 50 diapers a month per baby, which doesn’t cover the entire cost for diapers. But it does make the monthly diaper tab less daunting. “Diapers are expensive, and they just add to the cost of everything else,” she said. The diaper bank gets a large portion of its supply from the National Diaper Bank Network, buying bulk from manufacturers and regional diaper drives. Mary Kay Link, an Idaho Diaper Bank board member for seven years, sees how the organization helps mothers and families. She volunteers with the Holy Apostles St. Vincent de Paul of Meridian , one of 43 working partners that distribute diapers. “SVDP has many single moms who work and need food and diapers to make ends meet. Saving money on diapers allows them to use the money to pay bills or put gas in their car,” she said. Noble has been the executive director for almost a year, and demands for the service are growing. “When the diaper bank started in 2014, they were giving out 8,000 diapers a month, and when I started it was 50,000 per month. Typically, we give out 75,000 to 100,000 per month … last month we gave 119,000.” Noble says that level of growth would not happen without her board of directors. “We have an incredible all-volunteer board that has helped shape Idaho Diaper Bank into what it is today,” she said. “I would not be in the position I am today, or able to do what I do, without the support, leadership and willingness to jump in wherever they are needed.” The diaper bank’s 43 partners also contribute to the success. Susan Rohrbacher sees the needed help through Parma Community Schools, which serves more than 25 babies per month. “This partnership has been especially meaningful for families of children with special needs,” she said. “The Idaho Diaper Bank is truly making a difference by easing financial stress and helping our families feel supported and cared for.” As with other nonprofit organizations, Noble sees challenges. “The biggest need is sustainable funding that allows us to grow our reach. Our funding comes from grants and in-kind donations. There is no government assistance,” she said. “Simply put, if we want to send more diapers out the door, we have to bring more diapers and funding in the door,” Noble said. “Space is becoming another challenge. As we think about serving more families and potentially expanding, sustainable funding and the capacity to store the product becomes increasingly important.” One big way individuals and businesses can help is through diaper drives. “Some of my favorite moments are seeing people in the community rally around a diaper drive,” she said. “Those drives bring in product and monetary donations, of course, but they also get people talking about diaper needs and introduce people to our mission. It’s pretty incredible to watch.” The Idaho Diaper Bank is living up to its slogan, “Changing Babies. Changing Lives.” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE

items.title: Marsing, Homedale consider arming staff members
items.summary: Trained staff members could carry guns in the Marsing and Homedale school districts if local leaders move forward with safety programs modeled after one in the Kimberly district . As first reported by the Owyhee County Avalanche, Marsing Superintendent Norm Stewart and Homedale Superintendent Rob Sauer will present policies to their respective school boards this month that would lay out trainings
items.body: Trained staff members could carry guns in the Marsing and Homedale school districts if local leaders move forward with safety programs modeled after one in the Kimberly district . As first reported by the Owyhee County Avalanche, Marsing Superintendent Norm Stewart and Homedale Superintendent Rob Sauer will present policies to their respective school boards this month that would lay out trainings for staffers selected to carry concealed firearms. Sauer will propose a policy for armed staff at a Monday, Oct. 12, board meeting. Stewart will propose a similar policy to Marsing trustees at a Tuesday, Oct. 13, meeting. Marsing’s plan would reflect Kimberly’s policy “ as much as possible,” Stewart said. That could mean adopting it entirely. Sauer said Homedale intends to do the same. The Kimberly district, located near Twin Falls, rolled out its program last year and modeled it after one at Xavier Charter School. In August, a gunman killed three people at an In-N-Out drive-thru in Twin Falls. At least three school shootings have occurred in Idaho throughout the last four decades, but none have resulted in a death. Most recently, in 2021 , a Rigby sixth grader shot two students and a custodian. All three victims survived non-life-threatening injuries. “ This is not something we’re excited about,” Sauer said. “ We just recognize the times we live in, and that we need to do our best to deter and delay so law enforcement can do their job and protect our students.” The policies would allow some staffers to carry concealed firearms on campus, Stewart and Sauer said. Staff members would first need an enhanced concealed carry permit from the county. County sheriffs issue the permits. In Owyhee County, where Marsing and Homedale are located, residents fill out a form to receive a permit. Staff members would then have to volunteer to carry a concealed weapon and receive approval from the school board. They would undergo a physical fitness exam, and the districts would hire a third party to perform psychological evaluations. Once volunteers pass their tests, they would begin 40 hours of training. Marsing and Homedale have not identified who would train the volunteers, but they anticipate working with the Owyhee County Sheriff’s Office. Volunteers would then have to complete at least 16 hours of additional training each year. The districts would pay for training and ammunition but would not buy guns or pay volunteers for their training hours. Volunteers would not receive extra pay. “This is strictly voluntary, and you’re doing it because you want to do it for the right reasons: protecting students and staff,” said Stewart. Neither superintendent had estimates for what the programs would cost. The programs are meant to supplement law enforcement, not replace it, district leaders explained. Armed staff members can buy time against an active shooter when police responses are slower in rural areas. Homedale has a police department of seven full-time officers, according to the agency’s website. Marsing has no police department, and the district’s school resource officer is an Owyhee County sheriff’s deputy, one of around 16 officers at the agency, according to 2024 budget reporting on Transparent Idaho . Gun ownership is prevalent in Idaho, where concealed carry is legal without a permit. A 2020 RAND Corporation study estimated around 0.6 guns per Idaho household. Guns are also a part of the state’s culture: In November, Idahoans will vote for the official state gun. School boards in some districts have allowed staff members to carry guns for more than a decade. In January, the West Ada district introduced armed security guards called “campus sentinels.” As state funding for schools stagnates and districts struggle to balance their budgets, school safety can take a hit. items.body: Idaho Speaker of the House Mike Moyle’s political action committee this month reported $43,440 in independent expenditures to support three Republican incumbents in swing districts. Moyle, R-Eagle, created Idaho Rising PAC in late 2023. During the 2024 election cycle, the PAC raised $467,286 and reported $431,984 in independent expenditures, including $321,000 in opposition to Proposition 1, the ranked-choice voting ballot initiative. This year, Moyle’s PAC isn’t raising or spending nearly as much on political ads. Here’s what this month’s filings show: $23,600 to support Rep. Mike Pohanka in District 26 Seat A Pohanka, seeking a second term, faces Democrat Anita Janis and independent Christian conservative Bella Schiffler. Click here to read more about the race. $11,340 to support Rep. Dustin Manwaring in District 29 Seat A Manwaring has served four terms in the House and faces a third matchup against Democrat Mary Shea, whom he defeated in 2024 by 10.4 percentage points. $8,500 to support Rep. Brandon Mitchell in District 6 Seat B Mitchell is running for a fourth term and will face Democrat Kathy Dawes in a rematch. He won in 2024 by 16.2 percentage points. Moyle’s PAC this year received contributions from Ketchum-based GR Squire LLC, developer Dan Richter, Idaho Realtors PAC, Marathon Petroleum Corp., Chevron, Big West Oil and Blue Cross of Idaho. Several other state legislators have PACs: Rep. Jordan Redman , R-Coeur d’Alene, spent $350,000 of his own money on the May primaries this year through his 36-18-1 Inc. PAC. Rep. Josh Tanner , R-Eagle, and Redman both lead the Idaho Summit PAC, which spent $217,757 on the primaries. Senate Pro Tempore Kelly Anthon , R-Declo, is chairman of Gem State Legacy Political Action Committee, which contributed $15,750 to candidates this year. Rep. Chris Mathis , D-Boise, registered Rising Tide Idaho PAC this year. He contributed $6,000 of his own money and has not reported any expenses.

items.body: Two former school board members are running for a vacant Senate seat in a west Boise swing district. Republican Sen. Codi Galloway did not seek re-election this year in District 15, opening the seat for a race between Democrat Nancy Gregory, who just ended a 24-year run as a trustee for the Boise School District, and Republican Desi Burbank, the secretary of the Idaho PTA who previously served as a school board member on a North Carolina military base. Gregory wants to bring her decades of experience with school governance to the Legislature. She advocated for Boise schools for 24 years, but said that won’t be her mission as a senator. “I’m not being elected as an advocate for Boise schools,” Gregory said. “That’s the set of trustees who are sitting. That’s their job. That’s not my job anymore. items.body: The rotunda of the Idaho Statehouse as seen on Jan. 14, 2026, in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) When two mental health clinic owners in Idaho set out to restore critical services for people with severe mental illness, they faced an uphill battle. The Idaho Legislature was gearing up for across-the-board budget cuts. But Laura Scuri and Ric Boyce armed lawmakers with information and data — and spent time talking to journalists when four patients died after the mobile treatment service had been cut. Ric Boyce, director of Mental Health Specialists, testifies before the Idaho Legislature’s Medicaid Review Panel on Dec. 15, 2025 in Rexburg. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun) The two often worked behind the scenes, directly with lawmakers instead of testifying before committees. “We formed individual relationships with half the Legislature pretty much,” Boyce recalled in an interview. In the end, the programs that they advocated served as a rare instance of a budget cut that state lawmakers reversed. On the final day of this year’s legislative session, Idaho Gov. Brad Little signed into law a bill that temporarily restored funding for the programs that the two providers pushed for: the Assertive Community Treatment program, a mobile program for people with severe mental illness, and peer support services, which helps people navigate treatment. After four patients died, Idaho governor approves restoring cut Medicaid mental health programs Now, a mental health nonprofit plans to honor the two. This week, the National Alliance on Mental Illness of Idaho plans to award them both the Kathie Garrett Impact Award, named after a former Idaho lawmaker. In a news release, the nonprofit said the duo’s advocacy “led to the return of those programs.” The award came as a surprise. “I don’t think either one of us were thinking for a second it’s something that would be noticed,” said Boyce, a clinical social worker who owns Mental Health Specialists, a clinic in eastern Idaho’s Chubbuck. “What was important to us was that we were able to get the clients we were working with back into the program they needed so badly. And that was enough.” Scuri, who co-owns Access Behavioral Health Services in Boise, said it’s her first award. “So it’s extra special to me — especially with the environment that we’re in, and all the changes,” she said. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Boyce said providers often feel like government decisions are final. But he said this experience tested that conception. “What I learned was that there are ways to make change happen even when it seems hopeless,” he said. But to do that, he said, requires a lot of work — and help. While he and Scuri were talking with lawmakers, he said they also found lawmakers coming to them for answers — to questions raised by community members in letters and direct outreach on all sorts of Medicaid changes, not just the cuts they were focused on. “Even individual advocacy, of sending a single letter, cumulatively had an effect. And those things were changing the minds of legislators,” Boyce said. Laura Scuri, co-owner of Access Behavioral Health Services, testifies before the Idaho Legislature’s Medicaid Review Panel in Rexburg on Dec. 15, 2025. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun) Their advocacy experience taught Scuri to approach change as a process. “And really understanding that, as you go through that process, it’s not always gonna feel like you’re gonna get that change,” she said. “And so really staying in it, even though it gets really hard, and there are times when you don’t think you can overcome all the barriers.” And she said education is a big part of advocacy. items.body: A nine-member committee will begin the search for a new University of Idaho president . The State Board of Education announced the committee Friday, marking the first significant public step in the search. Current U of I President C. Scott Green announced his retirement on Sept. 9 ; he will stay on as president at his alma mater until June 30. Two State Board members will head the search: Shawn Keough of Sandpoint will chair the committee, and Pete Koehler of Caldwell will serve as vice chair. Koehler is a U of I alum. Here’s a look at the rest of the committee members: Chandra Zenner Ford, the U of I’s senior associate to the president, and executive officer of the university’s Boise and Southwest Idaho center. Mya Pronschinske Groza, a U of I marketing professor, and associate dean of the College of Business and Economics. Bill Gilbert, a former State Board member and a 1997 U of I graduate. Phil Reberger, who served as chief of staff to former Idaho Gov. and Sen. Dirk Kempthorne and former Idaho Sen. Steve Symms. Reberger is a 1964 U of I graduate. Clint Marshall, chair of the University of Idaho Foundation. Mary Hasenoehrl, owner of GKH Farms and partner in Gross Farms, Wilder. Dave Whitehead, president of Schweitzer Engineering Laboratories, Pullman, Wash. “We are grateful to these Vandals and community leaders for agreeing to serve,” State Board President Kurt Liebich said in a news release. “President Green has put the university in a strong position, and we are committed to a thorough search that finds a leader who can build on that momentum.” The timetable for the search is not set. However, the U of I has said the State Board hopes to fill the post by spring, before Green’s retirement. Under a new state law , passed this year, the presidential search process is now almost entirely a closed-door process. After private meetings and interviews, the search committee will submit a sole finalist’s name to the State Board. If board members agree to the recommendation, the board can publicly name the finalist and make the hire within 10 business days. The law also sets the guidelines for the makeup of a search committee, composed of at least eight members. With nine members, the U of I committee is slightly larger than the minimum required by law.

(Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Two days after a grand jury indicted a former Idaho state government employee on two felony counts of misuse of public funds, a local judge dismissed the case — after a request from the prosecutor. The case marked the first criminal charges — and a rare public update — to emerge from a yearslong investigation launched by Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador that probed how the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare doled out $72 million in federal child care grants in 2021 and 2022. The official who was criminally charged, Ericka Rupp, oversaw the grant program. In the indictment, filed in Canyon County District Court last week, the grand jury charged Rupp with two felony counts of misuse of public funds and securities, for allegedly illegally authorizing, appropriating or otherwise misusing more than $300 of the government’s money. Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador speaks at the Idaho Medal of Honor ceremony held Sept. 1, 2026, at the Idaho Statehouse in Boise. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Attorney General’s Office) Labrador’s special prosecutor, Canyon County Prosecuting Attorney Christopher Boyd, told the Idaho Capital Sun that the amount of money allegedly misused was not specified in the indictment, but that it would’ve been an issue to determine during a potential trial. Boyd said he moved to drop the indictment based on feedback from jurors. “I, however, asked of them whether they felt the case was one worth pursuing in terms of resources,” Boyd wrote in a text message. “I truly wanted their opinion on this. They had spent several full days taking testimony. The majority of jurors felt my time was better spent focusing on the many other serious crimes they worked on.” For each count, the penalties could have been up to 14 years imprisonment and up to $10,000 in fines, according to state laws cited in the indictment. Rupp’s attorney, Scott McKay, declined to comment. In a Friday order, Third District Judge Thomas W. Whitney wrote he was dismissing the case upon the state’s request. The court hasn’t released records supporting the judge’s decision to dismiss the case. Special prosecutor Christopher Boyd argues in district court that the Idaho Office of the Attorney General should not pay legal fees associated with litigation that set to block the office’s civil subpoena. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun) Pending permission from the court, Boyd said he hopes to release a report with more details in the coming days. Department of Health and Welfare spokesperson Greg Stahl directed questions about the case to parties involved. “(The Department of Health and Welfare) takes seriously its responsibility to be a good steward of taxpayer dollars and remains committed to transparency, accountability, and the appropriate use of public funds,” Stahl said in a statement. items.body: Few things are bipartisan anymore, but on Monday, the U.S. Senate overwhelmingly agreed on a college athletics makeover. Jeramiah Dickey More money for student-athletes. Less money for agents. Fewer player transfers. Limits on conference realignment. Protections for the non-revenue Olympic sports that now exist — precariously — under the inescapable shadow of football. Would it all affect college sports in Idaho? Absolutely. And should you care about all of that, even if you don’t care about college sports? Also, absolutely. An athletic program isn’t an entity unto itself. Increasingly, colleges and universities are looking to athletics as a revenue generator. This isn’t new: athletic success has long equated to increases in applications, enrollment and donor support. Now, colleges and universities want to use their athletic facilities to rake in revenue, and not just on game day. They want their facilities to bring in concerts and corporate retreats and support lucrative on-campus development. That long game hinges on staying competitive on turf and hardwood. Which puts college athletics in the unnatural position of hoping Congress will come to the rescue. “We’re living insanity, and the fact that the federal government’s having to get involved at all, I think, tells that story,” Boise State University athletic director Jeramiah Dickey told EdNews Thursday. What happened in Congress, and what happens next Monday’s 77-22 Senate vote was noteworthy — especially considering how much the sponsors crammed into the Protect College Sports Act . Far from a do-nothing bill, it tries to solve all of college sports’ problems in one shot. One big change: The bill will allow a college to pay its student-athletes up to $49 million a year, shattering the current $21 million “revenue sharing” cap. That higher cap would apply to everyone — but practically speaking, it may only be an issue in the NCAA’s so-called “Power Four” conferences, the Big Ten, the Southeastern Conference, the Big XII and the Atlantic Coast Conference. Terry Gawlik University of Idaho athletic director Terry Gawlik doesn’t expect to see her Big Sky Conference brethren bumping up against a $49 million cap. “They can make the cap as high as they want it for the Power Four, but we’re never going to get to that level of paying student athletes,” she said this week. “So that’s not something that affects us daily.” But the $49 million cap could affect Boise State. The Broncos made the first 12-team College Football Playoff two years ago and are contenders again this year — and landing in the CFP will pit Boise State against big-money programs that could push up to the salary cap. (Boise State paid its student-athletes $10 million last budget year.) Dickey said he’s “not a huge fan” of the $49 million cap, but he’s glad to see the bill set some kind of maximum. Both Gawlik and Dickey like another key piece of the bill. It would allow student-athletes to transfer once in their college careers — and force repeat transfers to sit out a season. The limits on transfers will restore stability in the locker room, Gawlik said. In a related vein, Dickey likes the limited, five-year window for athletes to complete their playing careers. “This is a chapter,” he said. “This is not forever.” The bill also sidesteps a political minefield: state laws restricting transgender athletes. Brad Little, who signed the nation’s first transgender athletics ban into law in 2020 , that’s a non-negotiable, spokeswoman Emily Callihan said this week. “Gov. Little remains strongly committed to defending women’s sports,” she said. What happens next to this bill, and all its pieces, is anyone’s guess. items.body: The Idaho Education Association (IEA) is cutting about 13% of its staff and closing its regional offices, leaders of the statewide teachers’ union announced this week. The cost-cutting measures come after union members told IEA’s board of directors to take a closer look at the organization’s budget and after a new law restricting taxpayer support for teachers’ union activities took effect. IEA is eliminating four union organizer positions, according to Executive Director Paul Stark. It’s also closing five regional offices, “centralizing operations in its Boise office.” And it’s turning Summer Institute, an annual professional development event, into an every-other-year event. IEA’s board of directors announced the cuts in an email to union members Monday. The board includes two dozen people, most of whom represent nine different geographic regions of the state. “Over the summer, we, your elected Board of Directors, carefully considered several options, asked difficult questions, and made decisions to put IEA on stronger financial footing for the future,” the board’s email said. “These decisions were not made lightly. They affect people. People who have dedicated themselves to serving our members and our profession.” Paul Stark, executive director of the Idaho Education Association " data-large-file="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/Paul-Stark-701x1180.jpg" class="wp-image-44392 size-thumbnail" src="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/Paul-Stark-119x200.jpg" alt="" width="119" height="200" srcset="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/Paul-Stark-119x200.jpg 119w, https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/Paul-Stark-368x620.jpg 368w, https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/Paul-Stark-701x1180.jpg 701w, https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/Paul-Stark-913x1536.jpg 913w, https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/Paul-Stark-1217x2048.jpg 1217w, https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/Paul-Stark-scaled.jpg 1521w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 119px) 100vw, 119px" /> Paul Stark, executive director of the Idaho Education Association The cuts followed a directive from IEA’s Delegate Assembly, a gathering of hundreds of local union leaders, the email said. In April the assembly told the board to “thoroughly examine” IEA’s budget and ensure that the union was “operating within its means.” The board also considered “the challenges created by recent legislative policies, including House Bill 516 ,” the email said. Enacted during this year’s legislative session , House Bill 516 prohibited public schools from using taxpayer-funded resources, such as payroll systems, to accommodate union activities. The Delegate Assembly issued a vote of no confidence in Gov. Brad Little for signing the “union-busting” bill into law. It took effect July 1. It’s unclear to what extent HB 516 factored into the downsizing. Among other restrictions, the law prohibits school districts from using payroll systems to deduct union dues. Districts also can’t offer teachers paid time off to engage in union activities unless IEA reimburses the district. And districts can’t give the union teachers’ contact information without their consent. The Freedom Foundation — an anti-union think tank based in Olympia, Wash. — for years lobbied lawmakers to enact the restrictions after it published a report arguing that Idaho unions were benefiting from government funds, facilities, resources and personnel. IEA leaders have repeatedly said that the union doesn’t receive taxpayer funding. But Stark didn’t provide specifics on how the law factored into the layoffs and office closures. “Idaho students and educators are only one month into the new school year, so the full effects of HB 516 on public education and the IEA have yet to be seen,” he said in an emailed statement Wednesday.

items.body: A televised state superintendent’s debate is off, after incumbent Debbie Critchfield backed out this week. Critchfield, a Republican, had originally agreed to an Oct. 12 debate against Democratic nominee Becky Sundin Mitchell, sponsored by KTVB. Critchfield now says she will not appear unless a third-party candidate — Constitution Party nominee Teresa Roundy — is also on the stage. The news comes barely a week after Critchfield and Sundin Mitchell appeared at a debate co-sponsored by Idaho EdNews and The College of Idaho . Roundy did not qualify for the Sept. 22 debate, since her campaign did not meet the co-sponsors’ fundraising threshold. The KTVB debate had a similar fundraising threshold, one the station says it has had in place for decades . Roundy’s campaign has not raised or spent any money, according to Idaho sunshine reports. In a statement to KTVB, Critchfield said her decision “isn’t about avoiding a debate,” but is instead about respecting the voters and the process. “There are three candidates in this race, and I believe voters deserve the opportunity to hear from all three,” Critchfield said in a statement to KTVB. “It’s not my place — or anyone else’s — to decide for voters which candidates are viable enough to be heard.” In a statement, Sundin Mitchell said Critchfield should be willing to answer questions about her record. “KTVB set its criteria for participation, and her decision to withdraw means Idaho voters will no longer get the opportunity to hear the candidates answer questions side by side,” Sundin Mitchell said. “Debates matter because elected officials should be willing to defend their records directly to the people they serve.” With the KTVB debate cancelled, Critchfield and Sundin Mitchell will probably not square off again before the Nov. 3 general election. The candidates have no other debates scheduled in the remaining five weeks of the campaign. The cancellation continues what has become an election-year trend. Debates between statewide candidates, once commonplace, have been nearly nonexistent this fall. Several Republican incumbents have refused to debate their opponents — rejecting or ignoring invitations to joint events. Gov. Brad Little, U.S. Sen. Jim Risch and Attorney General Raúl Labrador are unlikely to debate their opponents before the election. Consequently, the League of Women Voters has instead sponsored open forums, not debates, for whichever candidates decide to attend. An Oct. 6 Boise forum will feature Democratic gubernatorial candidate Terri Pickens and independent candidate John Stegner; Little has not responded to the invitation. items.body: With help from the Legislature, Idaho’s largest school district has the lowest property tax rate in the state and can build two new buildings over the next year without increasing its local tax burden. At a time when bonds and levies are hard to pass, West Ada School District trustees on Monday night approved a complicated loan agreement that will give the district $56.4 million in cash. The money will help the district turn a vacant warehouse into a career and technical education center on Locust Grove and rebuild Lake Hazel Elementary, with both projects expected to open in fall 2027. The district will pay the loan off over 15 years with ongoing state facilities funding. West Ada CFO Dave Roberts said the district expects at least $35.8 million in sales tax every year from House Bill 292 , passed in 2023. The bill was designed to reduce school districts’ property tax burden. A fraction of that annual appropriation, $5.3 million, will pay off the loan without increasing property taxes. “It’s possible that with this type of funding that West Ada may be able to build buildings without ever going to taxpayers again,” Roberts told EdNews on Tuesday. The projects follow the district’s recent completion of Independence Elementary in Star, which was built with state modernization funds from House Bill 521 and without an increase in property taxes. In a student survey last fall, 46% of Notus junior high school and high school students listed mental health as a concern. District Superintendent Jen Wright thought she had found a partial solution. She wanted to use $60,000 in federal grants to hire a behavioral health coordinator for preschool through 12 th grade. But last week, legislators tabled the program, leaving Notus and nine other rural schools shut out on funding. “I was really thinking that we were going to get it,” Wright said in an interview Tuesday. “It’s just very disappointing.” Until last week, the Department of Health and Welfare was pursuing a $1.2 million behavioral health hub program — designed to offer optional in-person or telehealth services to students and families. The money was going to come from a fraction of Idaho’s $186 million federal rural healthcare transformation grant . The Legislature’s Rural Health Transformation Committee abruptly put the behavioral health hub proposal on hold Friday — shifting the $1.2 million out of the program. Committee members noted that the Legislature had rejected a similar proposal in 2024 . Before Friday’s vote, nine districts had applied for behavioral health grants: Aberdeen, American Falls, Cascade, Castleford, Garden Valley, Marsing, Notus, Snake River and Wilder. Heritage Academy Public Charter in Jerome also applied. All the applicants were rural — and some distance from the closest clinic. In Notus’ case, the nearest mental health services are in Caldwell, a half hour drive away. Aberdeen School District Superintendent Scott Muir was hoping to use a $110,000 grant to bridge the gap between his rural community and health services in American Falls, about 20 minutes away, and Pocatello, about 50 minutes away. The grant would have gone toward new mental health and wellness services, additional counseling support and facilities upgrades. “We believe these efforts would have had a meaningful impact on the overall well-being of our students and community,” Muir said in an email to EdNews Tuesday. Friday’s committee vote came as a surprise to Wright. She said she only learned Notus had lost out on its grant through EdNews’ coverage of the hearing. The sudden news means Notus will look for other options. A new partnership with Insight Counseling — a third party that already works with Marsing and Wilder — will provide Notus with a clinical counselor.
