items.body: Idaho showed a 66% rise of 18 and 19-year-old registered voters between 2018 and 2022. Then, in 2023, Idaho legislators passed new voting laws targeted at student voters. After the laws took effect, Idaho saw a 23% decline in 18- and 19-year-old registered voters. Idaho is now last in the nation in the percentage of 18-year-old registered voters compared to registered voters aged 45 and older. Despite zero evidence of Idaho students fraudulently using their student IDs to vote, the law removed student IDs as an acceptable form of identification. Previously, students could use their ID as a form of identification for registering to vote, and to vote on election day. BABE VOTE and the League of Women Voters of Idaho challenged the laws in court. However, our case was dismissed without a trial. If granted a trial, we would have shown evidence of legally eligible Idaho voters who were unable to vote under the new laws. Upon pushback from the community, Representative Brent Crane (R-Nampa) who helped pass the laws, said,“[the laws] were doing exactly what they were designed to do.” We continue to hear positive messages from our Secretary of State about how easy it is for Idahoans to register and vote. But for some legally eligible Idahoans, it has not been easy. Although these laws specifically targeted students, they have created barriers for other Idahoans—including people who have moved, changed their names, or no longer drive. Sam Sandmire, a BABE VOTE member, spent more than an hour on the phone with the Secretary of State’s staff troubleshooting the system as she tried to change her address on her voter registration. It took her more than a week and additional phone calls before she was able to request an absentee ballot. This is not a one-time occurrence. Many long-time voters have reported that they have been removed from the voter database, even though they have voted consistently in recent elections. So these are not hypothetical concerns. They are issues we are hearing about and experiencing ourselves. If voters are unaware of potential problems or delays, they may wait until it is too late to resolve them. BABE VOTE does not want to discourage anyone from registering or voting. Our goal is to warn legally eligible voters to start now: check your voter registration, register or re-register to vote, and make a plan to vote, whether by absentee ballot, early in person, or at the polls on Election Day. Idahoans should not have to navigate unnecessary obstacles to exercise their right to vote, but until those obstacles are addressed, voters need to know they exist. Voting should not be a last-minute scramble. Don’t wait until Election Day. Check your registration, make a plan, and give yourself time to resolve any problems so you can cast your ballot. Babe, VOTE! BABE VOTE is a non-partisan, non-profit that empowers young people to organize their communities for democracy.

items.body: The Senate has overwhelmingly endorsed a far-reaching and bipartisan bill to overhaul college sports. Idaho Republican Sens. Mike Crapo and Jim Risch both voted for the Protect College Sports Act of 2026 , which passed Monday on a 77-22 vote . The bill still allows “revenue sharing,” direct payments to athletes. The spending cap would increase from $21.5 million to roughly $49 million, ESPN reported . Other provisions of the bill would allow student-athletes to transfer only once in their college careers; cap fees to agents at 5%; and restrict colleges and universities from cutting programs in Olympic sports in order to sink the savings into football. “College athletics are facing significant challenges Congress can and must meaningfully address,” Crapo said in a news release Tuesday. “The Protect College Sports Act provides much-needed clarity and consistency for student athletes and higher education institutions.” In the same news release, Idaho’s three university presidents took turns hailing the bill. “The Protect College Sports Act is an important pathway for creating a stable, fair foundation for college athletics,” Boise State University President David Hahn said. Despite the overwhelming Senate vote — and backing from President Donald Trump — the Protect College Sports Act is not a done deal. It still needs to pass the House, which is on recess until after the November election. If the House fails to act on the bill during a lame-duck session after the elections, ESPN noted, the process would have to start over in the next congressional session. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Ahead of the 2026 general election, Idaho election officials mailed out hundreds of thousands of informational pamphlets to households across the state. The state’s official voter pamphlet has already started to arrive at some households, the Idaho Secretary of State’s Office announced. 2026 Voter Guide Dates to know, how-to instructions and candidate surveys for Idaho’s top contested primaries. Read More The voter pamphlet includes information about the range of questions on the ballot — such as Proposition 1, a ballot initiative that would end the state’s abortion ban and establish reproductive rights; a proposed constitutional amendment that would only allow the Legislature to legalize drugs, such as marijuana; a constitutional amendment that would declare English as the state’s official language; and an advisory question that solicits a public vote to declare a state gun. That’s along with information about key upcoming election dates, voting options and voter registration. (You can also find information about those issues, along with races for statewide constitutional offices and in select legislative districts, in the Idaho Capital Sun’s voter guide .) “Election season is underway,” Secretary of State Phil McGrane, a Republican running for re-election, said in a statement. “Every household in Idaho can expect to receive a Voter Pamphlet with the information you need to be ready to vote in November. This special America 250 edition includes some fun nods to our history as we celebrate 250 years of America and make our mark on the future of our state. Make a plan, get registered, and vote!” To view the pamphlet online and access it in Spanish or an audio format, visit VoteIdaho.gov , a website run by the Secretary of State’s Office. That’s also where voters can see what their ballot will look like, along with other election resources. The voter pamphlet does not include information about candidates. In 2023 and 2024, the Idaho Legislature did not approve McGrane’s proposed bill to replace the voter pamphlet with a voter guide, which would include information about candidates. (Photo by Jordan Gale/Oregon Capital Chronicle) A new data center campus could soon be coming to federal land near Hermiston in eastern Oregon. It would be the first in Oregon sited on federal public land, and one of at least 12 proposed for more than 17,500 Bureau of Land Management acres across western states under President Donald Trump’s July 2025 executive order to hasten data center development. The proposals on federal land in Arizona, Idaho, Nevada, Oregon, Utah and Wyoming were first reported last week by The Washington Sun, whose reporters reviewed difficult to find right-of-way requests via BLM’s Mineral and Land Records System . The bulk of federally managed land in the U.S. is in the West, including in Oregon where half the state’s land is owned and managed by the federal government. Oregon is among the top 10 markets for data centers in the U.S., according to Pew Research. Under the executive order, Trump mandated that federally owned land and resources be used for “the expeditious and orderly development of data centers (…) to be used in service of the prosperity and security of the American people.” It’s the first time the Bureau of Land Management, tasked with managing more than 245 million public acres for uses that include animal grazing, timber harvesting and recreation, has been ordered to include data centers in its portfolio. Several months after Trump issued the order, the California-based energy company Copia, which has an office in Lake Oswego, submitted an application to site the Charlestown Data Center and Battery Energy Storage System in Umatilla County on 106 acres of BLM land. The company most recently submitted a draft plan for development of the data center project on May 8, 2026, available only via federal public records request, according to Sarah Bennett, a spokesperson for the bureau’s Northwest region office. items.body: An independent conservative running in a swing district against a Republican incumbent and a Democratic challenger means anything could happen in November. Rep. Mike Pohanka, R-Jerome, narrowly won the 2024 general election over Democrat Ned Burns by 2.4 percentage points. Pohanka now faces a three-way race against a Democrat with a long career in education and a Christian conservative independent who believes the government has turned away from God. Pohanka is seeking a second term in District 26 House Seat A. District 26 includes blue voters in Blaine County and red voters to the south in Jerome and Lincoln counties. But Pohanka said he considers himself colorblind. He said he’s a public servant who wants to help his constituents. “I have people coming up to me saying, ‘You know what? I’m a Democrat, and I’m voting for you because you are a person that cares and you’re doing the job,'” Pohanka said. That attitude encouraged independent Bella Schiffler to run. She interned for two lawmakers in Boise and said she learned that many politicians who call themselves conservative aren’t really conservative. Schiffler said education has become “woke,” citing a debunked hoax about litter boxes in schools. She told EdNews that she would be in favor of taking away women’s right to vote if it helped the country move closer to God. “America is a Christian nation, and we are founded on godly principles,” Schiffler said. Pohanka said he hopes Schiffler will not split the conservative vote in November, which happened two years ago when her aunt, Kala Tate, ran for the Senate as an independent. Anita Janis, chair of the Jerome County Democrats, wants to bring her experiences of teaching around the country to the Legislature. She said Idaho can learn from other states, where education funding works differently. “I have lived in other states where there would never be a levy put together to support salaries,” Janis said. She wants to see the Legislature fulfill its duty under the Idaho Constitution to fund public schools. Election Day is Nov. 3. items.body: U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright (center) visits Idaho National Laboratory with Idaho Gov. Brad Little (right) in December 2025. (Photo courtesy of Sarah Wood/U.S. Department of Energy) Editor’s Note: This is the first installment of a three-part Idaho Capital Sun series examining the proposal to bring a new Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus to Idaho. Part one focuses on Gov. Brad Little’s role in negotiations and his priorities for Idaho. The series continues Monday and Tuesday with a closer look at the cases for and against bringing a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus to Idaho. Idaho Gov. Brad Little said he will not jeopardize the health of the Eastern Snake Plain Aquifer or the health of Idahoans as he continues to negotiate potentially bringing a new Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus to Idaho. “I’ve had this direct conversation with Secretary (of Energy Chris) Wright: Disposal of spent fuel over the aquifer in Idaho – that’s a nonstarter,” Little said in an interview Wednesday at the Idaho State Capitol in Boise. In July, U.S. Department of Energy officials announced that Idaho is one of five states selected as a finalist to host one of the new innovation campuses. Little signed a memorandum of understanding in July with the U.S. Department of Energy, or DOE, to hold formal discussions and negotiations about bringing an innovation campus to Idaho. The Eastern Snake Plain Aquifer is outlined in orange of this map of Washington, Oregon and Idaho. (Map courtesy of the U.S. Geological Survey) If Idaho is selected as a host site, the federal government has said the state will have to accept shipments of spent nuclear fuel and radioactive waste from other states. A Request for Information Response that Little signed and submitted to the federal government in March describes an accelerated process that takes “months rather than decades” to bring the “initial capabilities” of a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus online in 2027. But on Wednesday, Little said things aren’t moving that quickly. “There’s a long way to go before this happens,” Little said. “(The DOE) would love to identify some sites, and I believe … they may need something by the end of the year. But it will not be in any way, shape or form a final agreement.” Little said the documents he signed do not obligate Idaho to host an innovation campus or accept nuclear fuel or radioactive waste. Instead, the agreements simply bring Idaho to the negotiating table, the governor said. Little said it makes sense for Idaho to be at the negotiating table because of the potential economic benefits to the state, the infrastructure, the experience at Idaho National Laboratory in eastern Idaho and the need for additional, reliable energy. The memorandum of understanding lists a Sept. 30 deadline, but Little said he doesn’t think agreements will be reached that quickly, and he suggested the two sides could either continue talks or sign another memorandum of understanding with a later deadline. Officials at Idaho National Laboratory declined to comment for this series of articles. What is a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus? There are now five other potential host sites for one or more DOE innovation campuses – Utah, Tennessee, Oklahoma, Louisiana and West Virginia. The Idaho Innocence Project helped secure Fain’s certificate of innocence and identify the true perpetrator, but was not involved in his original exoneration. Charles Fain says his three favorite letters in the alphabet are D-N-A. In 2001, Fain was exonerated and released from an Idaho prison after nearly 20 years on death row for a rape and murder he did not commit, using DNA analysis. After his release, the Idaho Innocence Project helped police identify the true perpetrator and got Fain a certificate of innocence and compensation for wrongful conviction. The Idaho Innocence Project has been shuttered for more than two years because of a lack of funding. However, on Sept. 17, Fain joined Innocence Project founder Greg Hampikian and fellow exoneree Amanda Knox to usher in a new group continuing the work of overturning wrongful convictions. The Innocence Center board member and exoneree Amanda Knox and retired founder of the Idaho Innocence Project Greg Hampikian. Hampikian lent his DNA expertise to Knox’s defense team to help free her from an Italian prison. (Photo by G Kenny3 Photography) Knox sits on the board of The Innocence Center , a nonprofit, free law firm based in San Diego that will take on cases in Idaho to try and free wrongfully convicted inmates. Hampikian, a forensic DNA expert, also lent his expertise to Knox’s defense team in the highly publicized case and helped free her from an Italian prison after she was wrongfully sentenced for the murder of her roommate while studying abroad. “It would be a desperate situation if these projects didn’t exist,” Knox said in an interview last week in Boise. “And when I heard that the Idaho Innocence Project was shutting down, I was really, really worried for the state of Idaho, because who else is going to do it?” The Innocence Center Executive Director Mike Semanchik was admitted to the Idaho bar on Sept. 18 so that he may work as an attorney for these cases in Idaho. “We’re committed to making this happen and making sure that wherever there are innocent people in prison, there’s an organization to support them,” Semanchik told a small gathering last week to kickoff the new work. Hampikian said he personally selected The Innocence Center to take up the work. “My last great act, after 20 years of the Innocence Project, was to choose a successor,” Hampikian said. “… (Semanchik) said, ‘I’ll get barred in Idaho, and I’ll take the cases until we raise the money.’ And I was like, ‘Oh, this guy’s got skin in the game.’” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. items.body: The Idaho Rural Health Transformation Program Implementation Task Force meets on Sept. 23, 2026, in Boise. (Photo by Laura Guido/Idaho Capital Sun) A group of rural Idaho hospital leaders, state officials and tribal representatives met for the first time Wednesday to oversee the process of awarding nearly $190 million in federal rural health grants. The Idaho Rural Health Transformation Program Implementation Task Force received an update on the state’s administration of the federal Rural Health Transformation grant program — a nationwide $50 billion, five-year federal grant Congress approved through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act last year. Idaho Department of Health and Welfare Director Juliet Charron. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare) “We are building and flying the plane at the same time. That feels like it’s been the consistent theme of this,” Idaho Department Health and Welfare Director Juliet Charron said Wednesday. The task force is meant to provide input on the process of implementation, help navigate potential challenges, and ensure the state is balancing statewide initiatives with actual needs of rural communities, Charron said. The nearly 20 funding opportunities posted by the state have closed, and Health and Welfare staff are reviewing applications to award subgrants. The opportunities include funding to provide school-based family support, chronic disease prevention and cancer screening, a cognitive care network, and diabetes prevention and management. The agency awarded national nonprofit Comagine Health with a grant to create a collaborative system to improve maternal and child health statewide, according to the program website. The state is nearing an Oct. 30 deadline to award all of the $186 million received for the first year of the program. “It is going to be a very, very tight timeline coming up to the end,” Charron said. For a health provider infrastructure opportunity, which will be about $97 million of the total grant, Charron said the agency received more than 250 applications asking for a total of more than $300 million. “That means that we will have to say no to some,” she said. Idaho submitted its first required report to the federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid, which is overseeing the program, on Aug. 31. The report will help determine how much funding the state gets in the second year of the five-year program. Charron said that the state hasn’t heard feedback on that report yet. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. (Photo by Hayat Norimine/KFF Health News) This story was first published by KFF Health News on Sept. 22, 2026. Joshua and Ashley Durham run a family medicine practice, and for the first time in their lives, they have no health insurance. When the Durhams began their practice at the end of 2023 — he as a primary care physician and she as a pharmacist who handles the billing — the couple bought coverage for themselves and their two kids on the Affordable Care Act marketplace. But they said their monthly premiums for a similar health plan for this year rose several hundred dollars to nearly $1,600. Top insurance official recommends task force for studying Idaho’s most critical healthcare issues They decided to pay out-of-pocket for their medical expenses instead, leaning on $50,000 they had set aside in a health savings account over several years. “It’s nerve-racking,” said Joshua Durham, 47. “It just takes, you know, one little accident, and then you got a big fat bill.” The healthcare industry traditionally has more of its workforce on medical insurance than many other fields. Nationwide, 7% of all healthcare workers were uninsured in 2024, compared with 11% of all adults under 65, according to a KFF analysis of the most recent American Community Survey data. And doctors were especially unlikely to forgo health insurance, with just 2% uninsured. But even healthcare workers are feeling the pinch as health insurance costs rise each year, with employers expecting that costs will jump an additional 8.2% for 2027. The Republican-led Congress also opted last year not to renew Affordable Care Act marketplace credits enacted during the covid pandemic. While subsidies remain in place for people with low incomes, the pandemic-era credits helped reduce many consumers’ premium payments , especially those working in small businesses such as independent medical practices. Nearly half of marketplace enrollees worked for small businesses or were self-employed in 2024; some of the most common occupations included chiropractic care and dentistry. Jack Dillon, executive director of the Association for Independent Medicine , which represents 4,000 physician-led practices, said premium increases have become untenable for small businesses, whether employers seek coverage through the marketplace or directly from insurers. “The cost has become so astronomical,” Dillon said. “You’re looking at it and saying, ‘What’s the value?’” As health insurance continues to become less affordable, Dillon said, more healthcare employers may seek alternatives to their standard coverage, such as providing higher hourly wages or providing only minimal plans. items.body: The Ninth U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals as photographed on June 12, 2017, in San Francisco, California. A panel of Ninth Circuit judges heard arguments Tuesday in a lawsuit challenging Idaho's abortion ban, seeking expanded exemptions. (Photo by Justin Sullivan/Getty Images) A panel of federal appeals judges will soon decide whether to continue to allow full enforcement of Idaho’s abortion bans, or to allow a lower court’s previous ruling that provided more exemptions to the law. U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit Judges Kim McLane Wardlaw, Marsha Berzon and Consuelo Callahan heard oral arguments in a virtual hearing Tuesday afternoon. The state of Idaho, represented by an attorney from the conservative Christian legal advocacy group Alliance Defending Freedom , argued that the laws should be fully enforced as written. Idaho’s laws prohibit most abortions, except in cases to prevent the death of the mother or in cases of rape and incest in the first trimester with a police report. Doctors face felony penalties and civil lawsuits of a minimum of $20,000 if they perform the procedure outside those exemptions. ADF attorney Mathew Hoffmann argued that a lower court’s previous ruling that would’ve expanded exemptions to apply to serious health and mental health risks to the mother, was not grounded in historical precedent. He said there is no right to “therapeutic” abortions. Attorneys representing Boise maternal-fetal medicine specialist Dr. Stacy Seyb argued that an earlier court decision from U.S. District of Idaho Judge B. Lynn Winmill should go back into effect. The ruling would’ve prevented the Ada County prosecutor and Idaho attorney general from enforcing Idaho’s abortion ban in cases where the mother’s health faced serious risk or her life was at risk due to self harm. Winmill later narrowed this block on enforcement to only protect abortions performed by Seyb. Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador. (Photo courtesy of Attorney General Raúl Labrador) After Attorney General Raúl Labrador appealed, a Ninth Circuit panel placed a hold on Winmill’s order, and the law went back into effect. Hoffmann said Winmill’s decision expanding the exemptions created “an abortion-on-demand regime.” “They leave it up to the subjective judgment of doctors to determine a risk sufficient to justify abortion,” he said. Stephanie Toti, executive director of the Lawyering Project, argued on behalf of Seyb that the expanded exemptions to the law were necessary. “The injunction entered by the district court in this case is narrow. It would enable only a small number of patients each year to obtain an abortion,” Toti said. “But for those patients, access to that care is vitally important, as the district court found.” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. Hoffmann argued that it would not, because the Constitution does not explicitly provide a right to abortions. Toti argued that the 2022 decision did not mention rights to life and health, which she said are violated by the Idaho ban’s limited exemptions. (Photo by Getty Images) A new gathering aims to bring together policymakers, students and the public to discuss the U.S. Constitution’s protections for fr
items.body: The inaugural Idaho Free Speech Summit will take place on Oct. 13 in Boise through the partnership of the Secretary of State's Office, the University of Idaho's College of Law and Boise State University's Institute for Advancing American Values. (Photo by Getty Images) A new gathering aims to bring together policymakers, students and the public to discuss the U.S. Constitution’s protections for free speech and encourage civil discourse. The inaugural Idaho Free Speech Summit will take place on Oct. 13 in Boise through the partnership of the Secretary of State’s Office, the University of Idaho’s College of Law and Boise State University’s Institute for Advancing American Values , according to a Secretary of State’s Office press release. The keynote speaker for the event will be Utah Gov. Spencer Cox, who has championed Disagree Better, a national, nonpartisan initiative “designed to reduce inflammatory rhetoric and foster a culture of healthy debate,” according to its website. Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane. (Photo courtesy of Phil McGrane) “Free speech is fundamental to our system of government, but protecting it requires more than simply agreeing that it is important,” said Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane. “It means listening to people we disagree with, defending their right to speak, and being willing to have difficult conversations. That is what we hope to accomplish with the Idaho Free Speech Summit.” Sessions at the summit will explore First Amendment issues “ranging from campaign finance and campus free speech to the broader challenges of maintaining civil discourse in an increasingly divided political environment,” the press release said. Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson (left) listens as Gov. Spencer Cox holds a press conference to present his budget proposal at the Salt Lake County Library in Kearns, Utah, on Dec. 3, 2025. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch) Cox will talk about how Americans can disagree without abandoning strongly held beliefs, a theme he explores in his new book, “Off Ramp: How to Be a Peacemaker in an Age of Contempt,” according to the release. “We are pleased to be part of a discussion centered on one of our nation’s most important constitutional freedoms,” said Brian Kane, University of Idaho College of Law dean, in the release. “The University of Idaho College of Law is a natural partner for this conversation. Law schools should be places where difficult constitutional questions are examined carefully and where people learn how to engage seriously with ideas they may not share.” The daylong summit will have presentations and panel discussions, followed by an evening reception. A continuing legal education credit will also be available for participating attorneys. “Universities have an important role to play in creating spaces where people can wrestle with difficult questions and hear perspectives different from their own,” said Boise State University’s Andrew Finstuen in the release. “The Summit provides an opportunity to model the kind of thoughtful, constructive dialogue that is essential to a healthy civic culture.” Registration and additional information, including the Summit schedule and speaker lineup, are available at FreeSpeechIdaho.com . “Our goal isn’t to bring together people who all agree,” McGrane said in the release. “It is to bring together people who recognize that our constitutional freedoms are strongest when we defend the right of others to speak, listen to one another, and engage in good faith.” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES.
